_README: Every field marked [YOU WRITE] or [YOU CITE] is yours to fill in from the course readings and your notes. The course prohibits generative AI on submitted work — keep timestamped drafts of all prose. Coordinates and dates are pre-filled as a starting reference; verify against your readings and adjust as you see fit.

miss-sarajevo.artist: Passengers (U2 & Brian Eno) feat. Luciano Pavarotti

eras.title: American Slavery
commentary: ~1.8 million died on the Middle Passage
~4 million enslaved in the U.S. by 1860
Resisters: Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Nat Turner, Denmark Vesey, John Brown
Ended legally with the 13th Amendment (1865); Black Codes, convict leasing, and Jim Crow followed
eras.scaleStat: ~12.5 million Africans trafficked across the Atlantic (1525-1866)

events.name: Point Comfort
events.summary: The English ship White Lion lands ~20 enslaved Africans at Point Comfort, VA — the conventional starting point of African slavery in British North America.

events.name: Stono Rebellion
events.summary: The largest slave uprising in the 13 colonies; ~20 enslaved people killed and triggered the harsh 1740 Negro Act.

events.name: Three-Fifths Compromise
events.summary: The Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia counts each enslaved person as 3/5 of a person for representation — embedding slavery into US founding law.

events.name: Haitian Revolution
events.summary: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue revolt and ultimately found Haiti (1804). Kendi tracks how white slaveholders in the US weaponized fear of 'another Haiti' to tighten slave codes.

events.name: Denmark Vesey
events.summary: Free Black carpenter Denmark Vesey's planned Charleston uprising is uncovered and crushed; 35 executed. Charleston builds the Citadel in response.

events.name: Nat Turner's Rebellion
events.summary: Nat Turner leads the deadliest slave revolt in US history in Southampton County, VA — ~60 white casualties; brutal reprisals follow and Southern states pass laws banning Black literacy and assembly.

events.name: Dred Scott v. Sandford
events.summary: Supreme Court rules Black Americans 'had no rights which the white man was bound to respect' and Congress cannot bar slavery in territories — pushing the country toward civil war.

events.name: Harpers Ferry
events.summary: Abolitionist John Brown raids the federal armory at Harpers Ferry attempting to arm an enslaved uprising. He is captured and hanged; the raid polarizes North and South.

events.name: Emancipation Proclamation
events.summary: Lincoln's wartime order declares enslaved people in Confederate states 'forever free' — recasts the Civil War as a war over slavery and authorizes Black enlistment.

events.name: 13th Amendment
events.summary: Lee surrenders at Appomattox; the 13th Amendment is ratified in December, abolishing slavery 'except as a punishment for crime' — a clause Kendi traces directly into convict leasing and Jim Crow.

eras.title: Native American Dispossession
commentary: Trail of Tears (1838-39): ~4,000 of 16,000 Cherokee died en route
Wounded Knee Massacre (1890): ~250-300 Lakota killed
~90 million acres taken under the 1887 Dawes Act
~150,000 Native children forced into federal boarding schools

eras.title: Segregation & Civil Rights
commentary: ~6 million Black Americans moved North in the Great Migration
Killed: Emmett Till, Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, MLK, the four girls in the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing
Leaders: King, Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, John Lewis, Fannie Lou Hamer
Segregationists: Bull Connor, George Wallace, Orval Faubus

eras.title: Eugenics
commentary: T4 program murdered ~250,000-300,000 disabled people in Germany
Buck v. Bell (1927): Supreme Court upheld forced sterilization 8-1
U.S. architects: Charles Davenport, Harry Laughlin, Madison Grant
Targeted: poor whites, Black, Latina, and Native women, the disabled, immigrants
eras.scaleStat: ~70,000 sterilized in the U.S.; ~400,000 sterilized in Nazi Germany

events.name: Indiana Sterilization Law
events.summary: Indiana becomes the first U.S. state — and the first jurisdiction in the world — to enact a compulsory sterilization law, targeting 'confirmed criminals, idiots, rapists and imbeciles' in state custody.

events.name: California Sterilization Act
events.summary: California passes its sterilization law and goes on to perform roughly 20,000 forced sterilizations through 1979 — one-third of the U.S. total. Coercive sterilization of Latina inmates in CA prisons continued until 2010.

events.name: Eugenics Record Office
events.summary: Charles Davenport founds the ERO at Cold Spring Harbor, NY with Carnegie Institution and Harriman funding. For three decades it drives American eugenic research, propaganda, and policy.

events.name: Passing of the Great Race
events.summary: Madison Grant publishes The Passing of the Great Race, popularizing 'Nordic' racial supremacy through Charles Scribner's Sons in New York. Hitler later called the book his 'Bible.'

events.name: Virginia Sterilization Act
events.summary: Virginia passes the Sterilization Act and the Racial Integrity Act in the same week — paired laws to legalize forced sterilization and outlaw interracial marriage on a 'one drop' rule.

events.name: Johnson-Reed Immigration Act
events.summary: Congress sets racially calibrated immigration quotas drawn directly from ERO superintendent Harry Laughlin's eugenic testimony, slamming shut U.S. borders to Southern and Eastern Europeans, Jews, and Asians.

events.name: Buck v. Bell
events.summary: Supreme Court upholds Virginia's forced sterilization of Carrie Buck 8–1. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.' Cited by Nazi defense attorneys at Nuremberg.

events.name: Nazi Sterilization Law
events.summary: Nazi Germany passes the 'Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring,' modeled on Laughlin's American template. About 400,000 Germans were sterilized by 1945.

events.name: Aktion T4
events.summary: Hitler authorizes a covert mass-killing program of disabled Germans run from Tiergartenstraße 4 in Berlin. ~70,000 murdered by gas — providing the technical methods, personnel, and infrastructure later used in the Holocaust.

events.name: Skinner v. Oklahoma
events.summary: Supreme Court unanimously strikes down Oklahoma's Habitual Criminal Sterilization Act, recognizing procreation as a fundamental right and beginning the legal retreat from Buck v. Bell.

eras.title: The Holocaust
commentary: ~5 million other victims: Soviet POWs, Poles, Roma, disabled, gay men, political prisoners
Architects: Hitler, Himmler, Heydrich, Eichmann, Höss
Killing centers: Auschwitz (~1.1M), Treblinka (~900K), Belzec, Sobibor
Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944
eras.scaleStat: ~6 million Jews murdered — about 2/3 of European Jewry

events.name: Dachau
events.summary: The first Nazi concentration camp, opened 22 March 1933 outside Munich; the organizational and architectural prototype for the entire SS camp system.

events.name: Sachsenhausen
events.summary: Headquarters of the SS Concentration Camp Inspectorate north of Berlin; held political prisoners, Soviet POWs, and homosexual men.

events.name: Buchenwald
events.summary: Massive forced-labor camp near Weimar; more than 56,000 prisoners died here. Liberated by US forces 11 April 1945.

events.name: Mauthausen
events.summary: Granite-quarry slave-labor camp in Austria, classified by the SS as 'Stufe III' — the harshest category. Roughly 90,000 prisoners murdered.

events.name: Ravensbrück
events.summary: Largest concentration camp for women in Nazi Germany; site of forced sterilization and medical experiments. ~30,000–50,000 dead.

events.name: Auschwitz-Birkenau
events.summary: Combined concentration and extermination camp in occupied Poland. About 1.1 million people were murdered here, the vast majority Jews gassed on arrival.

events.name: Bergen-Belsen
events.summary: Initially a POW and exchange camp; collapsed into mass death from typhus and starvation by 1945. Anne Frank died here weeks before British liberation in April 1945.

events.name: Chełmno (Kulmhof)
events.summary: The first dedicated Nazi extermination camp, using mobile gas vans. About 152,000 Jews and 4,300 Romani were murdered.

events.name: Majdanek
events.summary: Concentration and extermination camp on the outskirts of Lublin; ~78,000 dead. Captured nearly intact by the Red Army in July 1944 — first major camp seen by the Allies.

events.name: Bełżec
events.summary: First of the three Operation Reinhard camps; about 500,000 Jews killed in nine months. Dismantled by the Nazis in 1943 to hide the evidence.

events.name: Sobibór
events.summary: Operation Reinhard death camp; ~250,000 murdered. Site of a successful prisoner uprising on 14 October 1943 — one of only two camp revolts of the war.

events.name: Treblinka
events.summary: Operation Reinhard death camp east of Warsaw; ~900,000 Jews — including most of the Warsaw Ghetto — murdered in roughly 14 months.

eras.title: Japanese Biological Warfare & Pacific Atrocities
commentary: Unit 731 (Shiro Ishii): ~3,000 killed in experiments; ~200,000+ died from biological field tests
~200,000 women enslaved as 'comfort women' — mostly Korean and Chinese
Bataan Death March (1942): ~7,000-10,000 American and Filipino POWs killed
Unit 731 researchers received U.S. immunity in 1945 in exchange for their data
eras.scaleStat: ~200,000-300,000 killed at Nanjing; millions of Asian civilian deaths

events.name: Unit Tōgō
events.summary: Imperial Japan's first dedicated biological warfare facility, near Beiyinhe in Manchuria. ~1,000 Chinese prisoners experimented on before destruction in 1937.

events.name: Unit 731
events.summary: Major BW research and production complex at Pingfang under Gen. Shirō Ishii; at least 3,000 prisoners ('logs') killed in vivisection, frostbite, plague, and anthrax tests.

events.name: Nanking Massacre
events.summary: Six-week mass killing and rape after the fall of the Chinese capital; ~200,000–300,000 dead.

events.name: Ningbo Plague Attack
events.summary: Unit 731 drops plague-infected fleas from aircraft over the city — among the first deliberate biological attacks on a civilian population in modern history.

events.name: Bataan Death March
events.summary: ~76,000 American and Filipino POWs forced to march 65 miles to internment; thousands die en route from beatings, beheadings, and dehydration.

events.name: Comfort Women System
events.summary: State-organized military sexual slavery at peak; 50,000–200,000 women across occupied Asia, roughly 80% Korean.

events.name: US Immunity Deal
events.summary: MacArthur's occupation grants Ishii and Unit 731 leadership immunity in exchange for their biological warfare data — the central thesis of Harris's Factories of Death.

eras.title: Cambodian Genocide
commentary: S-21 prison (Tuol Sleng): ~14,000-20,000 prisoners; only ~12 known survivors
Leaders: Pol Pot, Nuon Chea, Khieu Samphan, 'Comrade Duch'
Targeted: intellectuals, monks, ethnic Vietnamese, Cham Muslims, urban dwellers
U.S. bombing (1969-73) helped destabilize the country
eras.scaleStat: ~1.7-2 million dead — roughly 1 in 4 Cambodians — in under 4 years

events.name: Phnom Penh Falls
events.summary: Khmer Rouge enters the capital on April 17; within hours forces ~2 million residents to evacuate to the countryside on threat of execution.

events.name: S-21 Tuol Sleng
events.summary: Former high school converted into the regime's central interrogation prison; ~14,000 detained, only 7 known survivors.

events.name: Choeung Ek
events.summary: 'Killing fields' execution site outside Phnom Penh; over 8,000 mass-grave victims excavated, including children killed by being beaten against trees.

events.name: Eastern Zone Purges
events.summary: Pol Pot accuses the Eastern Zone of disloyalty; ~100,000 cadres and civilians executed in internal purges through 1978.

events.name: Cham Massacres
events.summary: Systematic targeting of the Muslim Cham minority — forced renunciation of religion, executions; roughly half the Cham population dead by 1979.

events.name: Vietnamese Liberation
events.summary: Vietnamese forces capture Phnom Penh, ending the regime. Final toll: ~1.7–2.2 million dead, roughly 25% of the population.

eras.title: The Death Penalty
commentary: ~200 death-row exonerations since 1973 (DPIC / Innocence Project)
China executes ~1,000-8,000/year; Iran ~500-900
~41% of U.S. death row is Black (vs. ~13% of population)
Texas accounts for ~590 of post-1976 U.S. executions
eras.scaleStat: ~1,600 U.S. executions since 1976; thousands annually globally

events.name: First Gas Chamber
events.summary: Nevada becomes the first jurisdiction in the world to use lethal gas, executing Gee Jon at Carson City. Promoted as more 'humane' than hanging or electrocution.

events.name: Furman v. Georgia
events.summary: Supreme Court strikes down the death penalty as administered, finding it 'arbitrary and capricious' under the 8th Amendment. 629 inmates removed from death row; effective four-year moratorium.

events.name: Gregg v. Georgia
events.summary: Supreme Court reinstates the death penalty with new procedural safeguards — bifurcated trials, aggravating/mitigating factors, automatic appeal. The modern American death-penalty era begins.

events.name: Gary Gilmore Execution
events.summary: First execution after Gregg: Gilmore is killed by firing squad at Utah State Prison after demanding his own death and waiving further appeals. Subject of Norman Mailer's The Executioner's Song.

events.name: France Abolishes
events.summary: France becomes the last Western European country to abolish the death penalty, under Justice Minister Robert Badinter, ending a 189-year tradition of the guillotine.

events.name: First Lethal Injection
events.summary: Texas executes Charles Brooks Jr. by lethal injection at the Huntsville Unit — a method developed to be cheaper and less visually disturbing than the electric chair. Now used by every retentionist US state.

events.name: S v Makwanyane
events.summary: Post-apartheid Constitutional Court rules unanimously that capital punishment violates the rights to life and dignity in South Africa's new constitution. Mandela's first major rights ruling.

events.name: Atkins v. Virginia
events.summary: Supreme Court bars execution of intellectually disabled defendants as 'cruel and unusual.' Reverses 1989 Penry v. Lynaugh; states are left to define disability, producing wide variation.

events.name: Roper v. Simmons
events.summary: Supreme Court bars execution of offenders who were under 18 at the time of their crime, citing 'evolving standards of decency' and overwhelming international consensus.

events.name: Lockett Botched Execution
events.summary: Clayton Lockett's lethal injection at Oklahoma State Penitentiary fails after compounded drug substitutes cause a 43-minute death. Reignites the methodological and constitutional controversy over US executions.

eras.title: Refugees
commentary: Syria ~6.6M; Ukraine ~6.5M; Afghanistan ~6M; Venezuela ~7.7M
~1 million Rohingya in Cox's Bazar (Bangladesh)
~30,000+ have died on the Mediterranean crossing since 2014
Betts & Collier: the 1951 Refugee Convention is mismatched to today's protracted displacement
eras.scaleStat: 122+ million forcibly displaced (2024) — the highest in recorded history

eras.title: Watchwords: Torture, Hate Crimes, Gender Violence
commentary: U.S. hate crimes: ~11,862 incidents in 2023 (FBI) — record high
Guantánamo: ~780 detainees since 2002; ~30 remain
Abu Ghraib photos (2004) exposed by MP Joe Darby
OLC 'torture memos' (2002) by John Yoo and Jay Bybee authorized waterboarding
eras.scaleStat: ~1 in 3 women experiences gender violence; ~50,000 femicides per year

eras.title: Apartheid
commentary: Sharpeville (1960): 69 killed; Soweto Uprising (1976): ~176+ killed
~3.5 million Black South Africans forcibly removed under the Group Areas Act
Steve Biko killed in police custody (1977)
Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1995-2002) became the template for transitional justice
eras.scaleStat: ~21,000 deaths from political violence (1948-1994); 27 years for Mandela

events.name: National Party Victory
events.summary: Daniel Malan's National Party wins on a platform of formalized racial separation; apartheid begins as state policy.

events.name: Population Registration Act
events.summary: Every South African classified by race (White, Coloured, Indian, Black) — the foundation of all subsequent apartheid law.

events.name: Sharpeville Massacre
events.summary: Police fire on a peaceful pass-law protest, killing 69 and wounding 180. Triggers the banning of the ANC and PAC and Mandela's turn to armed struggle.

events.name: Rivonia Trial
events.summary: Mandela and seven co-defendants sentenced to life in Pretoria; Mandela's 'I am prepared to die' speech. Begins 27 years on Robben Island.

events.name: Soweto Uprising
events.summary: Students protest mandatory Afrikaans instruction; police kill ~176, including 13-year-old Hector Pieterson. Galvanizes the international anti-apartheid movement.

events.name: Steve Biko Killed
events.summary: Black Consciousness leader beaten to death in police custody, then transported 1,100 km naked in the back of a Land Rover. Subject of Peter Gabriel's 'Biko'.

events.name: Mandela Released
events.summary: After 27 years, Mandela walks free from Victor Verster Prison; F.W. de Klerk unbans the ANC, beginning the negotiated transition.

events.name: First Free Election
events.summary: Universal-suffrage election; Mandela elected president. Apartheid formally ends.

eras.title: Vietnam War & My Lai
commentary: +300,000 Cambodians and +50,000 Laotians killed by U.S. bombing
My Lai Massacre (March 16, 1968): ~504 unarmed villagers killed
Lt. William Calley convicted; Hugh Thompson Jr. landed his helicopter to stop the killing
Seymour Hersh broke My Lai; Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers (1971)
eras.scaleStat: ~58,220 U.S. dead; ~1-2 million Vietnamese civilian dead

events.name: US Combat Troops Land
events.summary: First US Marine combat units land at Da Nang; troop levels grow to 536,000 by 1968.

events.name: Tet Offensive (Hue)
events.summary: Coordinated North Vietnamese assault on 100+ cities; Hue occupied for 25 days, ~5,000 civilians executed by NVA. Shifts US public opinion against the war.

events.name: My Lai Massacre
events.summary: Charlie Company kills ~504 Vietnamese civilians (mostly women, children, elderly) in four hours. Hugh Thompson lands his helicopter to stop the killing.

events.name: Calley Court-Martial
events.summary: Lt. William Calley convicted of murdering 22 civilians at My Lai at Fort Benning; sentenced to life, paroled after 3.5 years under house arrest. Only conviction for the massacre.

events.name: Kent State
events.summary: Ohio National Guard kills four students protesting the Cambodian invasion. Subject of CSNY's 'Ohio'.

events.name: Pentagon Papers
events.summary: Daniel Ellsberg leaks the classified DoD history of US Vietnam involvement, revealing systematic government deception. NYT v. United States affirms press freedom.

events.name: Fall of Saigon
events.summary: NVA captures the South Vietnamese capital; helicopter evacuations from US embassy. War ends.

eras.title: The Troubles (Northern Ireland)
commentary: Bloody Sunday (Jan 30, 1972): 14 unarmed marchers killed by British paratroopers
1981 hunger strike: Bobby Sands and 9 others died in Maze Prison
Omagh bombing (Aug 15, 1998): 29 killed, including a woman pregnant with twins
Good Friday Agreement signed April 10, 1998

events.name: Derry Civil Rights March
events.summary: Police attack a Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association march in Derry, broadcast worldwide. Conventional start of the Troubles.

events.name: Bloody Sunday
events.summary: British paratroopers shoot 26 unarmed civilians at a civil-rights march in Derry, killing 14. Subject of U2's 'Sunday Bloody Sunday'.

events.name: Birmingham Pub Bombings
events.summary: IRA bombs in two Birmingham pubs kill 21. The 'Birmingham Six' wrongfully convicted; released 1991. Subject of In the Name of the Father.

events.name: IRA Hunger Strikes
events.summary: Bobby Sands and 9 others die on hunger strike at HM Maze demanding political-prisoner status. Sands elected to UK Parliament during the strike.

events.name: Warrington Bombings
events.summary: IRA bombs kill two children in Warrington; Cranberries' 'Zombie' written in response.

events.name: Omagh Bombing
events.summary: Real IRA car bomb kills 29 — deadliest single attack of the Troubles. Subject of the film Omagh.

events.name: Good Friday Agreement
events.summary: Multi-party agreement establishes power-sharing assembly and ends the Troubles. Approved by 71% of NI voters in referendum.

eras.title: Latin American Dictatorships

regions.name: Fort Benning, GA (School of the Americas)

commentary: Guatemala: ~83% of victims indigenous Maya (CEH truth commission)
El Salvador: ~75,000 killed; El Mozote massacre ~800-1,000 (1981)
Archbishop Óscar Romero assassinated March 24, 1980
U.S. School of the Americas (Fort Benning) trained many implicated officers
eras.scaleStat: Argentina ~30,000 disappeared; Chile ~3,200 killed; Guatemala ~200,000 killed

events.name: Pinochet Coup
events.summary: US-backed military coup overthrows Salvador Allende in Santiago; Pinochet's regime tortures and 'disappears' ~3,200 Chileans through 1990. Víctor Jara murdered four days later.

events.name: Argentine Dirty War
events.summary: Junta seizes power in Buenos Aires; ESMA naval academy becomes detention center. ~30,000 'disappeared' through 1983, including babies stolen from imprisoned mothers.

events.name: Romero Assassinated
events.summary: Archbishop Óscar Romero shot during Mass in San Salvador after publicly condemning state killings. Subject of the film Romero.

events.name: El Mozote Massacre
events.summary: US-trained Atlacatl Battalion of the Salvadoran army kills ~1,000 civilians, mostly children. Long denied by the US and Salvadoran governments.

events.name: Trial of the Juntas
events.summary: Argentina prosecutes its own former military leaders — first such trial in Latin America. Five junta members convicted.

events.name: Chilean Plebiscite
events.summary: 55% vote 'No' to extending Pinochet's rule; democratic transition begins. Pinochet later arrested in London (1998).

eras.title: Bosnian War & Srebrenica
commentary: Siege of Sarajevo: 1,425 days — the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare
20,000-50,000 women raped as a tool of ethnic cleansing
Convicted of genocide at the ICTY: Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić
Power: the Clinton administration evaded the word 'genocide' until after Srebrenica
eras.scaleStat: ~100,000 killed and ~2.2 million displaced; ~8,372 murdered at Srebrenica

events.name: Siege of Sarajevo
events.summary: Bosnian Serb forces blockade the city for 1,425 days — longest siege of a capital in modern history. ~13,952 killed, including 5,434 civilians.

events.name: Omarska & Trnopolje
events.summary: Bosnian Serb concentration camps near Prijedor; ITN footage of emaciated detainees evokes Auschwitz, ending Europe's 50-year 'Never Again.'

events.name: Markale Market Shelling
events.summary: Mortar attack on Sarajevo's central market kills 68 civilians; second attack in 1995 triggers the NATO air campaign.

events.name: Srebrenica Massacre
events.summary: Bosnian Serb forces under Ratko Mladić execute ~8,372 Bosniak men and boys after capturing the UN 'safe area.' First legally recognized European genocide since the Holocaust.

events.name: Dayton Accords
events.summary: 21-day negotiation at Wright-Patterson AFB ends the war and partitions Bosnia. Signed in Paris 14 December 1995.

eras.title: Rwandan Genocide
commentary: Fastest mass killing rate in modern history
RTLM 'hate radio' broadcasts incited the killing
UN commander Roméo Dallaire warned in advance and was overruled

events.name: Habyarimana Plane Downed
events.summary: April 6: surface-to-air missile downs the presidents of Rwanda and Burundi at Kigali airport — trigger for the genocide that begins within hours.

events.name: PM Uwilingiyimana Killed
events.summary: April 7: moderate Hutu prime minister and 10 Belgian UN peacekeepers murdered in Kigali; Belgium withdraws and the UN cuts UNAMIR from 2,500 to 270.

events.name: Nyarubuye Church
events.summary: April 15: Hutu militia and clergy massacre ~20,000 Tutsi who had taken refuge in the parish complex. Site now a national memorial.

events.name: Murambi Technical School
events.summary: April: ~50,000 Tutsi told to gather at the school 'for protection' and murdered over 24 hours. Bodies preserved as a national memorial.

events.name: Bisesero Resistance
events.summary: May–June: Tutsi farmers in the hills hold off Interahamwe attacks for two months armed with stones and farm tools; ~50,000 of 60,000 ultimately killed.

events.name: Operation Turquoise
events.summary: June: late French military 'humanitarian' intervention in western Rwanda — criticized for sheltering retreating génocidaires.

events.name: RPF Captures Kigali
events.summary: July: Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front takes the capital, ending 100 days of genocide. ~800,000 dead — three-quarters of the Tutsi population.

eras.title: Post-9/11: Iraq, Guantánamo, Abu Ghraib
commentary: ~7,000 U.S. troops killed; tens of thousands of post-9/11 veterans dead by suicide
Guantánamo: ~780 detainees since 2002; ~30 remain, most never charged
Architects: Bush, Cheney, Rumsfeld; 'torture memos' by John Yoo and Jay Bybee
Abu Ghraib photos exposed by MP Joe Darby (2004)
